title: Geometry
summary: Lines and angles, triangles and their four centres, similarity and BPT, Pythagoras, quadrilaterals, polygons and circles. The single largest advanced-maths block in CGL (3–5 questions per shift), and nearly every question runs off a memorised angle result, a triplet, or a ratio rule.

subtopics.title: Lines and angles
subtopics.concept:
At a point on a straight line the total angle is $180^\circ$; around a point it is $360^\circ$.
When two straight lines cross, the **vertically opposite** angles are equal.

For **parallel lines** cut by a transversal (the standard CGL figure):
- **Corresponding angles** are equal (both "top-right", etc.).
- **Alternate angles** are equal (Z-shape).
- **Co-interior (allied) angles** add to $180^\circ$ — this gives a small equation in $x$.

An **angle bisector** splits an angle into two equal parts; two bisectors of a triangle meet at the incentre.

formulas.name: Angles on a line / around a point

tricks.title: Co-interior gives the equation
tricks.body:
If two allied angles are given as expressions in $x$, set their sum to $180^\circ$, solve for $x$, then substitute
back into the angle asked.

example.q: Two co-interior angles between parallel lines are $(3x+20)^\circ$ and $(2x+10)^\circ$. Find the larger angle.

tricks.title: Supplement − complement one-liner
tricks.body:
For an angle $x$: supplement $=180-x$, complement $=90-x$, so the difference is always $90^\circ$, and the angle
itself is $\frac{180-d}{2}$ if the difference $d$ is given.

example.q: The supplement of an angle is four times its complement. Find the angle.

mistakes: Forgetting that co-interior angles are supplementary only between **parallel** lines.
Reading the wrong pair: alternate vs corresponding in the transversal figure.
Solving for $x$ and answering $x$ instead of the angle asked.

subtopics.title: Triangles and their centres
subtopics.concept:
Angle facts: the interior angles add to $180^\circ$; an **exterior angle equals the sum of the two remote interior
angles**. In an isosceles triangle the median to the base is also the altitude and the bisector.

**The four centres (memorise the angle results):**

| Centre | Defined by | Key result |
|---|---|---|
| Centroid G | medians | divides each median $2:1$ from the vertex |
| Incentre I | angle bisectors | $\angle BIC=90^\circ+\frac{A}{2}$ |
| Circumcentre O | perpendicular bisectors | $\angle BOC=2\angle A$ |
| Orthocentre H | altitudes | $\angle BHC=180^\circ-\angle A$ |

For a right triangle the orthocentre is the right-angle vertex and the circumcentre is the midpoint of the
hypotenuse; in an equilateral triangle all four centres coincide.

tricks.title: Centre angles from one input
tricks.body:
The asked angle involves $\angle A$ only. Read off which centre is drawn: bisectors → $90+\frac A2$,
perpendicular bisectors → $2A$, altitudes → $180-A$.

example.q: In $\triangle ABC$, $\angle A=70^\circ$. Find $\angle BHC$ where $H$ is the orthocentre.
example.solution: $\angle BHC=180^\circ-70^\circ=110^\circ$. (For the incentre it would be $90+35=125^\circ$; for the circumcentre $140^\circ$.)

tricks.title: Centroid ratios without coordinates
tricks.body: The centroid cuts each median in $2:1$ from the vertex. If the median is $3m$ long, the pieces are $2m$ and $m$.

example.q: The median $AD$ of $\triangle ABC$ is 15 cm. Find $AG$ where $G$ is the centroid.

tricks.title: Median by Apollonius or symmetry
tricks.body:
For an isosceles triangle skip the formula: the median to the base is $\sqrt{a^2-(b/2)^2}$.
Otherwise use $m_a^2=\frac{2b^2+2c^2-a^2}{4}$.

example.q: Find the median to the base of an isosceles triangle with equal sides 25 cm and base 14 cm.
Find the area of a triangle with sides 13, 14, 15 cm.

mistakes: $\angle BIC=90^\circ+\frac A2$ vs $\angle BOC=2A$ vs $\angle BHC=180^\circ-A$ get swapped under exam pressure.
Centroid ratio read the wrong way: $GD=\frac13 AD$, not $\frac23$.
Exterior angle taken at the wrong vertex — it equals the sum of the two **remote** interior angles.
Heron: forgetting to halve the perimeter before subtracting.

subtopics.title: Congruence, similarity and BPT
subtopics.concept:
**Congruence** (same size and shape): SSS, SAS, ASA/AAS, RHS.

**Similarity** (same shape): corresponding angles equal and sides in the same ratio. For similar triangles with
scale factor $k$:
- corresponding sides, perimeters, medians, altitudes → ratio $k$,
- areas → ratio $k^2$.

**Basic Proportionality Theorem (Thales):** a line parallel to one side of a triangle divides the other two sides
in the same ratio: $DE\parallel BC\Rightarrow\frac{AD}{DB}=\frac{AE}{EC}$.

**Midpoint theorem:** the segment joining midpoints of two sides is parallel to the third side and half its length.

tricks.title: Square the perimeter ratio for areas
tricks.body: Perimeters in ratio $p:q$ → areas in ratio $p^2:q^2$ (and back: side ratio $=\sqrt{\text{area ratio}}$).

example.q: Two similar triangles have perimeters 30 cm and 50 cm. If the area of the smaller is 18 sq cm, find the area of the larger.
example.solution: Side ratio $=\frac35$, so area ratio $=\frac{9}{25}$: larger area $=18\times\frac{25}{9}=50$ sq cm.

tricks.title: Midpoint theorem shortcut
tricks.body:
Spot the words "midpoints of two sides" → the joining segment is half the third side, parallel to it.
Conversely, through the midpoint of one side, parallel to another → it bisects the third side.

example.q: In $\triangle ABC$, $D$ and $E$ are midpoints of $AB$ and $AC$. If $DE=4.5$ cm, find $BC$.

tricks.title: BPT with a parallel drawn inside
tricks.body:
When a line parallel to a side cuts the other two sides, write the ratio directly. If the segments on one side
are $AD:DB=2:3$, the same ratio holds on the other side.

example.q: In $\triangle ABC$, $DE\parallel BC$ with $AD=4$ cm, $DB=6$ cm, $AE=5$ cm. Find $EC$.

mistakes: Using the side ratio (not its square) for areas — or squaring when you should not.
Taking $DE=\frac{BC}{2}$ as true for any parallel line; it needs **midpoints**.
BPT ratio written as $AD/AB=AE/AC$ carelessly — it is correct, but mixing $AD/DB$ with $AE/AC$ on opposite sides is the classic slip.

subtopics.title: Pythagoras theorem and triplets
subtopics.concept:
In a right triangle with hypotenuse $h$: $h^2=p^2+b^2$. The converse also holds — it is how CGL tests
"which triangle is right-angled". Memorise the standard **triplets** (and their multiples):
$$(3,4,5)\ (5,12,13)\ (7,24,25)\ (8,15,17)\ (9,40,41)\ (11,60,61)\ (12,35,37)\ (20,21,29)$$
Useful extras: median to the hypotenuse $=\frac{h}{2}$; the diagonal of a rectangle is $\sqrt{l^2+b^2}$; in an
obtuse triangle $a^2>b^2+c^2$ (acute if $a^2<b^2+c^2$) where $a$ is the longest side.

tricks.title: Triplet recognition
tricks.body:
See two numbers, recall the third: 12 and 13 → 5; 24 and 25 → 7; 15 and 17 → 8. Multiples scale: 6-8-10,
9-12-15, 10-24-26 are all 3-4-5 families.

example.q: A ladder 25 m long stands with its foot 7 m from a wall. How high does it reach?

tricks.title: Median to the hypotenuse is half of it
tricks.body:
In any right triangle the median from the right angle equals half the hypotenuse (three equal pieces:
the two half-hypotenuses and the median).

example.q: In a right triangle with hypotenuse 13 cm, find the median to the hypotenuse.

tricks.title: Converse: check $a^2$ vs $b^2+c^2$
tricks.body: To identify the right/obtuse/acute triangle, square only the longest side and compare.

example.q: Which of the triangles with sides (i) 6, 8, 11 (ii) 6, 8, 10 (iii) 6, 8, 9 is right-angled?

mistakes: Adding instead of subtracting: the unknown leg is $\sqrt{h^2-b^2}$, not $\sqrt{h^2+b^2}$.
Calling any big triangle right-angled without checking a triplet or the squares.
Half-hypotenuse median confused with the median to a leg.

subtopics.title: Quadrilaterals and polygons
subtopics.concept:
**Quadrilateral:** angles add to $360^\circ$. Key areas: parallelogram $=b\times h$; rhombus $=\frac12 d_1d_2$
(with side $=\sqrt{(d_1/2)^2+(d_2/2)^2}$); trapezium $=\frac12(a+b)h$. Diagonals of a rectangle are equal and
bisect each other; of a rhombus they bisect at right angles.

**Cyclic quadrilateral:** all four vertices on a circle; **opposite angles are supplementary**. Its area
(Brahmagupta) is $\sqrt{(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)(s-d)}$.

**Regular polygon** with $n$ sides: interior angle $=\frac{(n-2)180^\circ}{n}$, each exterior $=\frac{360^\circ}{n}$,
diagonals $=\frac{n(n-3)}{2}$.

tricks.title: Exterior angle → number of sides
tricks.body:
For regular polygons the exterior angle is the fastest route: $n=\frac{360^\circ}{\text{ext}}$, and
$\text{ext}=180^\circ-\text{int}$.

example.q: The interior angle of a regular polygon is $156^\circ$. How many sides has it?

tricks.title: Rhombus side from diagonals
tricks.body:
Half-diagonals form a right triangle with the side: side $=\sqrt{(d_1/2)^2+(d_2/2)^2}$. If the halves are 8 and 6,
the side is a 6-8-10 triplet.

example.q: The diagonals of a rhombus are 16 cm and 12 cm. Find its side.
example.solution: Halves 8 and 6 → side $=10$ cm (area $=96$ sq cm).

tricks.title: Diagonal count one-liner
tricks.body:
$n$ vertices, each joins $n-3$ others (not itself, not two neighbours), each diagonal counted twice:
$\frac{n(n-3)}{2}$.

example.q: How many diagonals does a decagon have?

mistakes: Rhombus area $\frac12 d_1d_2$ applied to a rectangle or parallelogram.
Cyclic quadrilateral: adding non-opposite angles to $180^\circ$.
Interior/exterior angle confused; also $(n-2)\times180^\circ$ misapplied as $n\times180^\circ$.

subtopics.title: Circles: chords, tangents, secants and cyclic angles
subtopics.concept:
**Chords:** a perpendicular from the centre bisects a chord; chord $=2\sqrt{r^2-d^2}$. Equal chords are
equidistant from the centre (and subtend equal angles at the centre).

**Angles:** angle at the centre $=$ twice the angle at the circumference on the same arc; angles in the same
segment are equal; the angle in a semicircle is $90^\circ$.

**Tangents:** tangent $\perp$ radius; the two tangents from an external point are equal; tangent–secant
$PT^2=PA\cdot PB$; two chords crossing inside give $p_1p_2=q_1q_2$.

**Cyclic quadrilateral:** opposite angles supplementary; the exterior angle equals the interior opposite angle.

**Common tangents of two circles** ($d$ = centre distance): separate ($d>r_1+r_2$) → 4; externally tangent → 3;
intersecting → 2; internally tangent → 1; one inside the other → 0. Direct tangent length
$=\sqrt{d^2-(r_1-r_2)^2}$, transverse $=\sqrt{d^2-(r_1+r_2)^2}$.

tricks.title: Triplet inside a circle
tricks.body:
$r$-$d$-$\frac{\ell}{2}$ is a right triangle: radius 13 and distance 5 → half-chord 12 → chord 24. Circles reuse
the same triplets as Pythagoras questions.

example.q: A chord is at distance 5 cm from the centre of a circle of radius 13 cm. Find its length.

tricks.title: Tangent–secant: multiply the pieces
tricks.body: Tangent squared = external secant × whole secant. Read the "whole" as external + internal part.

example.q: From P, a tangent of length 6 cm and a secant whose external part is 4 cm are drawn. Find the internal (chord) part.
example.solution: $6^2=4\times\text{whole}\Rightarrow$ whole $=9$, so the chord inside is $9-4=5$ cm.

tricks.title: Count common tangents from $d$ vs $r_1, r_2$
tricks.body:
Compare $d$ with $r_1+r_2$ and $|r_1-r_2|$: outside → 4, touching outside → 3, overlapping → 2, touching
inside → 1, contained → 0.

example.q: Two circles of radii 4 cm and 9 cm have centres 13 cm apart. How many common tangents do they have?

tricks.title: Concentric chord trick
tricks.body:
A chord of the outer circle tangent to the inner circle has length $2\sqrt{R^2-r^2}$ — the inner radius is the
distance from the centre to the chord.

example.q: Two concentric circles have radii 25 cm and 7 cm. Find the chord of the larger that touches the smaller.

mistakes: Forgetting to **double** the half-chord: $\sqrt{r^2-d^2}$ is only half the chord.
Tangent–secant: using the internal part instead of the whole secant length.
$d=r_1+r_2$ vs $d=|r_1-r_2|$ confusion changes the tangent count completely.
Angle in the same segment vs angle in the alternate segment mixed up.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Parallel lines with expressions in x
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A transversal across parallel lines with angles $(ax+b)^\circ$; find $x$ or the angle.
pyqPatterns.approach: Co-interior sum to $180^\circ$, corresponding/alternate are equal; solve the small equation and substitute back.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Angle result at a triangle centre
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: $I$/$O$/$H$ defined as incentre/circumcentre/orthocentre; $\angle A$ given, find $\angle BIC$, $\angle BOC$ or $\angle BHC$.
pyqPatterns.approach: $90^\circ+\frac A2$, $2A$, $180^\circ-A$ respectively. For bisectors of $B$ and $C$ directly: $90^\circ+\frac A2$.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Ratio of areas of similar triangles
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Perimeters (or sides/altitudes) of two similar triangles in ratio; find areas, or reverse.
pyqPatterns.approach: Perimeter ratio $k$ → area ratio $k^2$; invert with a square root when going from areas to sides.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Midpoints of sides, or a line parallel to one side cutting the other two.
Ladder, pole, diagonal, or circle radius–chord–distance; numbers like 13-12, 25-24, 17-15.
pyqPatterns.approach: Recognise the triplet and answer without computing squares; multiples of (3,4,5) are everywhere.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Regular polygon angle or diagonal count
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Interior angle given → find $n$; or diagonals of an $n$-gon.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Circle: tangent, secant or chord products
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Tangent from an external point, secant pieces, intersecting chords, concentric-circle chord.
Angles of a cyclic quadrilateral given as a ratio or one angle given.
pyqPatterns.approach: Opposite pairs sum to $180^\circ$: set up $k(a+c)=180^\circ$ or subtract the given angle from $180^\circ$.

solvedExamples.q: In $\triangle ABC$, $\angle A=50^\circ$. $BO$ and $CO$ are the internal bisectors of $\angle B$ and $\angle C$, meeting at $O$. Find $\angle BOC$.
solvedExamples.figure: <svg viewBox="0 0 250 190" width="250" stroke="currentColor" fill="none"><polygon points="115,30 35,165 215,140" stroke-width="1.5"/><line x1="115" y1="30" x2="122" y2="112" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/><line x1="35" y1="165" x2="122" y2="112" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/><line x1="215" y1="140" x2="122" y2="112" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/><text x="115" y="30" dx="-5" dy="-6" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif">A</text><text x="35" y="165" dx="-12" dy="-6" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif">B</text><text x="215" y="140" dx="2" dy="-6" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif">C</text><text x="122" y="112" dx="6" dy="8" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif">I</text></svg>
solvedExamples.solution:
$B+C=180^\circ-50^\circ=130^\circ$. The bisectors take half of each:

$\angle OBC+\angle OCB=\frac{B}{2}+\frac{C}{2}=\frac{130^\circ}{2}=65^\circ$.

So $\angle BOC=180^\circ-65^\circ=115^\circ$.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Memorise $\angle BIC=90^\circ+\frac{A}{2}=90^\circ+25^\circ=115^\circ$ — valid for the incentre, which is exactly where the two bisectors meet.

solvedExamples.q: Two similar triangles have areas of $16\ \text{cm}^2$ and $25\ \text{cm}^2$. If the perimeter of the smaller triangle is $32$ cm, find the perimeter of the larger triangle.
solvedExamples.solution:
Area ratio $=16:25$, so the side (and perimeter) ratio is $\sqrt{16}:\sqrt{25}=4:5$.

Larger perimeter $=32\times\frac54=40$ cm.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Areas → perimeters needs a square **root**: $\sqrt{16/25}=\frac45$. Traps: $32\times\frac{25}{16}=50$ (forgot the root), $32\times\frac45=25.6$ (inverted).

solvedExamples.q: From an external point $P$, a tangent $PT$ of length $12$ cm and a secant $PAB$ are drawn to a circle. If $PA=8$ cm, find the length of the chord $AB$.
solvedExamples.shortcut: $144/8=18$ is the **whole** secant; subtract the external part: $18-8=10$. Trap: 18 itself.

solvedExamples.q: The angles of a cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$ are in the ratio $1:2:3:2$ in that order. Find the largest angle.
solvedExamples.figure: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 205" width="260" stroke="currentColor" fill="none"><circle cx="130" cy="105" r="75"/><polygon points="59.5,79.4 104.35,175.5 200.5,130.65 155.65,34.5" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="59.5" y="79.4" dx="-16" dy="0" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif">A</text><text x="104.35" y="175.5" dx="-6" dy="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif">B</text><text x="200.5" y="130.65" dx="6" dy="4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif">C</text><text x="155.65" y="34.5" dx="0" dy="-6" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif">D</text></svg>
solvedExamples.solution:
Let the angles be $k, 2k, 3k, 2k$. Since $ABCD$ is cyclic, $A+C=180^\circ$:

$k+3k=180^\circ\Rightarrow k=45^\circ$.

Angles: $45^\circ, 90^\circ, 135^\circ, 90^\circ$. Largest $=135^\circ$.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Only **opposite** pairs must sum to $180^\circ$: $(1+3)k=180$ gives $k=45$; check $B+D=(2+2)\times45=180$ ✓. The largest is $3k=135^\circ$.

practice.q: Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. If two co-interior angles are $(3x+20)^\circ$ and $(2x+10)^\circ$, then the larger of the two angles is:
practice.solution: Co-interior angles add to $180^\circ$: $3x+20+2x+10=180\Rightarrow 5x=150\Rightarrow x=30$. The angles are $110^\circ$ and $70^\circ$; the larger is $110^\circ$.
practice.shortcut: $x=30$ at once ($150/5$); angle $=3(30)+20=110^\circ$. Answering $70^\circ$ or $x=30$ are the traps.

practice.q: In $\triangle ABC$ the interior angles at $A$ and $B$ are $52^\circ$ and $63^\circ$. The exterior angle at $C$ is:
practice.solution: The exterior angle at a vertex equals the sum of the two remote interior angles: $52^\circ+63^\circ=115^\circ$.
practice.shortcut: Add the two remote angles: $115^\circ$. (Computing $180-115=65^\circ$ gives the *interior* angle at $C$ — a trap.)

practice.q: A ladder 25 m long leans against a wall with its foot 7 m away from the base of the wall. How high up the wall does the ladder reach?
Each interior angle of a regular polygon is $156^\circ$. The number of sides of the polygon is:
practice.shortcut: $n=360/24=15$. Trap: $1560/... $ i.e. using $(n-2)180=156n$ directly is slower; and 13 (from $n=\frac{180}{180-156}$... just memorise ext route).
practice.pattern: regular polygon: interior angle to n

practice.q: A chord of a circle is at a distance of $5$ cm from the centre. If the radius of the circle is $13$ cm, the length of the chord is:
practice.solution: Half-chord $=\sqrt{13^2-5^2}=\sqrt{169-25}=12$ cm, so the chord is $24$ cm.
practice.shortcut: 5-12-13 triplet → half-chord 12 → chord 24 cm. Trap: 12 cm (forgot to double).

practice.q: In $\triangle ABC$, the median $AD$ from $A$ to $BC$ is $15$ cm long. If $G$ is the centroid of the triangle, then $AG$ is equal to:
practice.figure: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 200" width="260" stroke="currentColor" fill="none"><polygon points="130,30 30,170 230,170" stroke-width="1.5"/><line x1="130" y1="30" x2="130" y2="170" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/><line x1="30" y1="170" x2="180" y2="100" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/><line x1="230" y1="170" x2="80" y2="100" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/><text x="130" y="30" dx="-5" dy="-6" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif">A</text><text x="30" y="170" dx="-12" dy="-6" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif">B</text><text x="230" y="170" dx="2" dy="-6" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif">C</text><text x="130" y="170" dx="-4" dy="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif">D</text><text x="80" y="100" dx="-16" dy="0" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif">E</text><text x="180" y="100" dx="6" dy="0" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif">F</text><text x="130" y="123" dx="8" dy="4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif">G</text></svg>
practice.solution: The centroid divides each median in the ratio $2:1$ from the vertex: $AG=\frac{2}{3}\times15=10$ cm (and $GD=5$ cm).

practice.q: In $\triangle ABC$, $\angle B=55^\circ$ and $\angle C=45^\circ$. If $I$ is the incentre of the triangle, then $\angle BIC$ is equal to:
Two triangles are similar and their perimeters are $30$ cm and $50$ cm. If the area of the smaller triangle is $18\ \text{cm}^2$, the area of the larger triangle is:
practice.solution:
Side ratio $=\frac{30}{50}=\frac35$, so the area ratio is $\frac{9}{25}$.

Larger area $=18\times\frac{25}{9}=50\ \text{cm}^2$.
practice.shortcut: Area ratio $=(3/5)^2=9/25$; scale up: $18\times25/9=50$. Trap: $18\times5/3=30$ (used the linear ratio).
practice.pattern: similar triangles: perimeter ratio to areas

practice.q: In $\triangle ABC$, $D$ and $E$ are the midpoints of $AB$ and $AC$ respectively. If $DE=4.5$ cm, then $BC$ is equal to:
practice.solution: By the midpoint theorem, $DE\parallel BC$ and $DE=\frac{BC}{2}$. So $BC=2\times4.5=9$ cm.
practice.shortcut: Double it: 9 cm. Trap: 2.25 (halved instead of doubled).

practice.q: $ABCD$ is a cyclic quadrilateral in which $\angle A:\angle C=3:2$ and $\angle B=95^\circ$. The angle $\angle D$ is equal to:
practice.solution:
$\angle B$ and $\angle D$ are opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral, so $\angle B+\angle D=180^\circ$:

$\angle D=180^\circ-95^\circ=85^\circ$.
practice.shortcut: The $3:2$ data is a distractor — only $\angle B$ and $\angle D$ are opposite, so $180-95=85^\circ$. (Ratios would matter only if $\angle A$ were asked: $108^\circ$.)

practice.q: Point $P$ is at a distance of $13$ cm from the centre $O$ of a circle of radius $5$ cm. The length of the tangent drawn from $P$ to the circle is:
practice.figure: <svg viewBox="0 0 250 175" width="250" stroke="currentColor" fill="none"><circle cx="65" cy="105" r="50"/><line x1="65" y1="105" x2="185" y2="105" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/><line x1="185" y1="105" x2="85.8" y2="59.5"/><line x1="65" y1="105" x2="85.8" y2="59.5"/><text x="65" y="105" dx="-14" dy="6" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif">O</text><text x="185" y="105" dx="2" dy="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif">P</text><text x="85.8" y="59.5" dx="-4" dy="-6" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif">T</text></svg>
practice.solution: The radius to the point of contact is perpendicular to the tangent: $PT^2=OP^2-OT^2=169-25=144$, so $PT=12$ cm.

practice.q: The diagonals of a rhombus are $16$ cm and $12$ cm. The length of each side of the rhombus is:
practice.solution:
The diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other at right angles. Half-diagonals are $8$ and $6$:

side $=\sqrt{8^2+6^2}=10$ cm.
practice.shortcut: 6-8-10 triplet → 10 cm. Trap: 14 (half the sum of half-diagonals... i.e. averaging), 20 (using full diagonals as legs).

practice.q: Two concentric circles have radii $25$ cm and $7$ cm. A chord of the larger circle touches the smaller circle. The length of this chord is:
practice.figure: <svg viewBox="0 0 300 195" width="300" stroke="currentColor" fill="none"><circle cx="150" cy="105" r="68"/><circle cx="150" cy="105" r="19"/><line x1="84.7" y1="86" x2="215.3" y2="86"/><line x1="150" y1="105" x2="215.3" y2="86" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/><text x="150" y="105" dx="4" dy="6" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif">O</text><text x="84.7" y="86" dx="-14" dy="0" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif">A</text><text x="215.3" y="86" dx="2" dy="-4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif">B</text><text x="150" y="86" dx="-6" dy="-6" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif">M</text></svg>
practice.solution:
The radius of the smaller circle is the distance from the centre to the chord. Half-chord
$=\sqrt{25^2-7^2}=\sqrt{625-49}=24$, so the chord is $48$ cm.
practice.shortcut: 7-24-25 triplet: half-chord 24 → chord 48 cm. Trap: 24 cm (half only).

practice.q: In an isosceles triangle $ABC$, $AB=AC=25$ cm and $BC=14$ cm. The area of the triangle is:
practice.solution:
The median/altitude to the base: $h=\sqrt{25^2-7^2}=24$ cm.

Area $=\frac12\times14\times24=168\ \text{cm}^2$.
practice.shortcut: 7-24-25 again: height 24, area $=\frac12\times14\times24=168$. Trap: 336 forgot the $\frac12$.

practice.shortcut: $d=13$, $r_1+r_2=11$: $\sqrt{13^2-11^2}=\sqrt{48}=4\sqrt3$. Trap: $\sqrt{105}$ is the **direct** tangent $\sqrt{169-8^2}$. Both tangent types exist since $13>11$.
